title: Luttinger v. Rosen
summary: A home buyer who diligently sought the specified mortgage could recover the deposit when no qualifying loan was available; the seller’s later offer to subsidize a different loan did not satisfy the condition.
notes: The notes ask whose performance the condition protects and whether a buyer choosing to pay cash could insist on completion. They also invite comparison with the risk of dealing with an individual financier rather than a bank. Those questions should be analyzed separately from the holding.

sections.Parties: The Luttingers were buyers of a house. The Rosens were the sellers who retained the buyers’ deposit after the proposed sale failed.
sections.Material Facts:
The parties agreed on an $85,000 purchase price and an $8,500 deposit. The purchase depended on the buyers obtaining a $45,000 first mortgage from a bank or other lending institution for at least twenty years at an interest rate no higher than 8.5 percent. The buyers promised to use due diligence. The agreement provided for a refund and termination if the buyers could not obtain that financing and gave timely notice.

The buyers relied on an attorney familiar with available lending terms. He applied to the only institution that would then make a loan of the required size on a single-family house. It offered a loan at the prevailing rate at closing, with a minimum of 8.75 percent. The buyers gave timely notice and requested their deposit. The sellers subsequently offered an unspecified funding arrangement to make up the interest difference over twenty-five years. The buyers declined that substitute.
sections.Procedural History: The buyers sued for return of their deposit and prevailed. The Connecticut Supreme Court affirmed, rejecting the sellers’ challenges to diligence and to the failure of the mortgage condition.
sections.Issue: Did an unsuccessful application to one bank satisfy the buyers’ diligence obligation, and could the sellers compel completion by offering to subsidize a nonqualifying loan?
sections.Holding: The buyers used due diligence, the specified financing condition did not occur, and the buyers were entitled to the refund. The sellers’ proposed subsidy did not change that result.
sections.Reasoning:
The attorney’s knowledge of the lending market supported the finding that additional applications would have been futile. Due diligence did not require pointless applications. This was a finding based on the evidence about available loans, rather than a general rule that one application always suffices.

The agreement made a particular type of institutional financing a condition of the buyers’ obligation to complete the purchase. An offer requiring at least 8.75 percent failed that condition. A private promise to reimburse the excess interest was a different arrangement, even if its expected financial effect could be similar. The buyers had performed their separate duty to try, so failure of the condition released them from completing the purchase under the terms the parties chose.

textbookImport.basis: Study paraphrase of the supplied tenth-edition casebook. No current-law/citator review.

learning.why: This case separates a duty to make reasonable efforts from a condition that those efforts must actually produce a particular result. It also demonstrates how conditions allocate financing risk.

topics.conditions: The specified mortgage had to become available before the buyers were obliged to complete the purchase.
topics.interpretation: The court enforced the actual institutional-financing terms rather than substituting an economically similar arrangement.
topics.discretion: The buyers’ ability to withdraw was constrained by a separate duty to seek the loan diligently.
topics.restitution: The agreement required return of the deposit when the financing condition failed after diligent efforts.

mnemonic.rationale: A mortgage the buyer could not get
